overview: Ambocas names an Indigenous population and a colonial province in Ecuador’s Loja region. Colonial writers connected the population with Cañari ancestry, but this name does not identify a precisely bounded kingdom with a known founding and fall.

periods.title: Ambocas in the encomienda system
periods.summary: Loja’s municipal history records the assignment of the Ambocas encomienda to Felipa Arias Castillo around 1565. Santiago and neighboring settlements appear within this colonial provincial setting, after Spanish rule had transformed local institutions.

periods.title: Leaders challenge tribute demands
periods.summary: A cataloged letter from leaders of Ambocas and neighboring communities complained that tribute accounts still included absent and dead people. They asked the Audiencia to investigate the accounts and abuses.

periods.title: A disputed colonial appointment
periods.summary: A request to confirm Alonso de Benavides as lieutenant of Ambocas was rejected. The catalog records an objection based on the prohibition against appointing such officers in Indigenous towns.

periods.title: Antonio Montoya petitions over forced service
periods.summary: Antonio Montoya, identified as cacique of Ambocas, complained that a priest compelled him to perform stable, household and baking work. The record preserves his challenge, without establishing its outcome.

items.text: Loja’s municipal account of Santiago de Ambocas describes fields, grazing land, woodland and accessible water in a cool environment. Its language about supposedly unused land reflects a colonial assessment of usefulness. Such a description helps reconstruct a farming landscape, but is not a neutral survey of Indigenous land rights.

A colonial observer distinguished Ambocas builders who laid adobe from other workers who made the blocks. Brito Román cites this account in discussing Cañari connections. It provides evidence for skilled building labor, while the observer’s ethnic ranking should not become a judgment of people’s abilities or worth.

The municipal history of El Cisne says difficult, steep terrain led colonial authorities to allow community land beyond the usual surrounding allocation. The account links settlement with the practical need for usable ground. It does not provide enough surveyed evidence to reconstruct every boundary on this map.

El Cisne’s account describes Indigenous residents commissioning a Virgin Mary image from Diego de Robles in 1595. The carved cedar sculpture connects local patrons with a wider colonial artistic world. Accounts of an apparition belong to devotional tradition; they are not archaeological proof of when Ambocas people first occupied the region.

sections.title: What petitions reveal about daily life

items.text: The February 1639 letter from leaders of Ambocas, Calbas, Paltas, Chuquiribamba and Malacatos challenged excessive tribute. The catalog describes their complaint that rolls had not been corrected for people who were absent or dead. Household obligations depended on records, so outdated lists could impose burdens on those who remained.

Those petitioners asked for an Audiencia official to examine the accounts and presented their request as beneficial to the royal treasury. The document’s description shows coordinated advocacy across communities and an understanding of colonial procedures. It does not tell us whether the requested investigation occurred or whether payments were reduced.

Antonio Montoya’s 1787 petition concerns concrete work: caring for horses, domestic service and baking for the local priest. Identified as a cacique, he appealed to the dignity of his position. The catalog preserves his allegation of compelled service, not a court finding that independently verifies every detail.

The rejected 1732 appointment of a lieutenant in Ambocas illustrates conflict within colonial administration. The corregidor’s nomination faced a legal objection before the Audiencia. Formal restrictions on officials could create grounds for resistance, although this one case cannot establish that communities were consistently protected from interference.

sections.title: Reading changes in population and identity

items.text: El Cisne’s municipal history attributes severe population losses to smallpox and measles. It also distinguishes surrounding communities such as Ari, Ganajapa and Nona. A count of tribute-paying people at a settlement would exclude others, so it should not be turned into a complete census or a claim that all Ambocas vanished.

Brito Román discusses a Cañari connection and possible Inca-era resettlement, while comparing different proposed locations for Ambocas. Resettlement is an interpretation of historical testimony, not a directly dated migration recovered by excavation. The surviving name does not establish that provincial and ethnic boundaries were identical.

Santiago’s municipal history cites a 1778 census organized by Pedro Xavier de Valdivieso y Torres. It is evidence for a particular settlement under colonial rule. A town census should not be used as the population of every community associated with the larger Ambocas province.

ending.text: Colonial government reorganized Ambocas communities through tribute, labor and church institutions. This research has not established a single ending year for their collective identity. Brito Román records Ambocas heritage among the traditions claimed by Loja’s modern communal federation. The map’s 1500 cutoff is not evidence of extinction.
